name: Cooling eye mask

lead: A cooling eye mask is a gel pad or packet chilled in a fridge or freezer and placed over the closed eyes. People use it in the morning to reduce temporary puffiness around the eyes and look more awake.

Cold causes vasoconstriction and slows fluid buildup, so eyelids look less swollen after several minutes, and gentle pressure from the pad may help. Guidance from eye-care and consumer health sources supports cold compresses for transient swelling; no peer-reviewed trial of these masks was found. The effect is short-lived and cosmetic.

paras: People keep the mask in the fridge or freezer and lie back with it over closed eyes for around ten minutes after waking, often before skincare or makeup. Many use it a few mornings a week or after a short night.

Applying ice directly to eyelids can injure skin, so a barrier and short use are advised. Persistent, one-sided, painful, or vision-affecting swelling is advised to be medically reviewed, as it may indicate infection or other disease. The mask is not reported to change eye bags that are structural or fat-related.

angle.text: Users chill a gel mask and rest it over closed eyes in the morning to cut puffiness around the eyes for the next few hours. Cold narrows surface vessels and slows fluid buildup, a principle widely used for short-term swelling.

lead: A cooling eye mask is a gel pad, gel-filled packet or similar pack that is chilled, usually in a refrigerator or freezer, and placed over the closed eyes. In appearance-focused communities it is used mainly in the morning with the aim of reducing temporary puffiness around the eyes over several minutes.

The effect that users seek is short-lived and cosmetic. No peer-reviewed trial of these masks for periorbital puffiness was found in the sources reviewed, so claims about their effect rest on the general principle that cold constricts blood vessels and on consumer experience.
infobox: Chilled gel or foam eye pack
Short morning application over closed eyes

paras: Common designs are reusable gel packs in a fabric or plastic shell, sometimes shaped to fit the orbit and held with an elastic strap, and gel sheets or patches that are chilled before use. Patent literature describes a related concept, an eye pack for evaporative cooling of the area around the eyes made of a gelatinous foam impregnated with an aqueous polyvinyl alcohol solution and fitted with a barrier that lets heat pass but restricts transfer of the solution [1]. That filing, from 2011, shows that such devices have been the subject of commercial design work, though a patent is not evidence of effectiveness.

The proposed mechanism is vasoconstriction: cold narrows small blood vessels and slows the accumulation of fluid in the loose tissue of the eyelids, so that morning swelling looks reduced after a short application. Gentle pressure from the pad is also said to help. These mechanisms are general physiological explanations commonly given in consumer guidance, and no study of cooling eye masks in the sources reviewed measured them.

Eye-care and consumer health guidance generally advises against applying ice directly to the eyelids because very cold surfaces can injure skin, and recommends a barrier such as a cloth and short application times. Swelling that persists, affects one side, is painful or involves vision changes is generally regarded by clinicians as needing medical assessment because it may reflect infection or other disease. Eye bags that are structural or related to fat, rather than temporary fluid, are not expected to respond to cooling.

Cooling masks are discussed as a quick, inexpensive morning step for puffy eyes alongside sleep position, sleep duration and skincare routines. Price points are commonly quoted at about $10 to $25. Because the effect described is temporary, it is distinct from treatments aimed at the longer-term structure of the under-eye area.
